questions.question: Why does Postgres recommend JSONB over JSON for almost all use cases?
options: JSONB preserves the original text formatting exactly as typed
JSONB decomposes the document into a parsed binary tree, removing whitespace and sorting keys, which enables GIN indexing and faster repeated queries
JSONB is the only type that can store nested objects
JSONB documents are always smaller than JSON documents on disk
questions.explanation: JSON stores the literal text you inserted and must be re-parsed from scratch on every query, with no support for indexing. JSONB decomposes the document into a binary tree at insert time -- stripping insignificant whitespace and sorting keys -- which both avoids repeated re-parsing and exposes a structure that GIN indexes can operate on for fast containment and key-existence queries.

questions.question: What is the practical difference between `info->'specs'` and `info->>'name'`?
options: There is no difference; both always return text
`->` returns the value still wrapped as JSON/JSONB (useful for chaining further into nested objects), while `->>` returns the value as plain TEXT (useful for direct comparisons)
`->>` only works on arrays, not objects
`->` is faster than `->>` in every case
questions.explanation: `->` extracts a value but keeps it as a JSON/JSONB type, which is exactly what you want when drilling further into a nested structure, e.g. `info->'specs'->>'res'`. `->>` extracts a value and casts it directly to TEXT, which is what you need for equality comparisons like `WHERE info->>'name' = 'TV'` since comparing a quoted JSON string against an unquoted text literal would otherwise fail to match.

questions.question: Your queries against a JSONB column exclusively use the `@>` containment operator. Which GIN operator class should you choose and why?
options: jsonb_ops, because jsonb_path_ops does not support @> at all
jsonb_path_ops, because it indexes only the values reachable by path, producing a smaller and typically faster index for containment-only workloads
Neither -- B-Tree is required for @> queries
It does not matter; both operator classes produce identical index sizes
questions.explanation: jsonb_path_ops indexes only the values reachable through their path in the document (not every key separately), which produces an index roughly 40% smaller than the default jsonb_ops and is typically faster for @> containment lookups. The trade-off is that jsonb_path_ops supports @> only -- it cannot accelerate key-existence operators (?, ?|, ?&). If your workload needs those too, jsonb_ops is the right default despite its larger size.

questions.question: A GIN index was created as `USING GIN(info jsonb_path_ops)`. A new query uses `WHERE info ? 'beta_opt_in'`. What happens?
options: The query uses the existing index efficiently
Postgres throws a syntax error
The planner falls back to a sequential scan, because jsonb_path_ops does not support the `?` key-existence operator
The index is automatically rebuilt with jsonb_ops
questions.explanation: jsonb_path_ops only supports the @> containment operator -- it does not index keys in a way that the ? (key-existence) operator can use. When a query uses an operator unsupported by the available index's operator class, the Postgres planner correctly falls back to a Seq Scan rather than silently returning wrong results. The fix is to add a second GIN index using the default jsonb_ops operator class alongside the existing jsonb_path_ops index, since Postgres can maintain multiple indexes on the same column for different operator needs.

questions.question: Why does updating a single key inside a large JSONB document cause 'write amplification'?
options: Because JSONB documents are compressed and decompression corrupts unrelated keys
Because Postgres's MVCC model never edits rows in place -- every UPDATE writes an entirely new row version, so changing one key forces the entire document to be rewritten to disk
Because GIN indexes must be dropped and recreated on every UPDATE
Because JSONB columns are stored as multiple separate rows internally
questions.explanation: Postgres uses MVCC (Multi-Version Concurrency Control), meaning UPDATE never modifies bytes in place -- it always creates a new row version and marks the old one as a dead tuple for later vacuuming. For a JSONB column, this means even a one-key change requires writing out the full document again, not just the changed bytes. A 50 KB profile updated 1,000 times a day therefore writes roughly 50 MB of new data daily purely from that one column's churn, which is why frequently-updated fields should be pulled out into dedicated columns instead.

questions.question: What does the `?` operator test for, and when is it useful?
options: It tests whether a value is NULL anywhere in the document
It tests whether a specific top-level key exists in the JSONB document, regardless of that key's value -- useful for optional-field queries in schema-less designs
It is a wildcard match operator equivalent to LIKE '%pattern%'
It tests whether the document is valid JSON syntax
questions.explanation: The ? operator checks purely for the presence of a top-level key, independent of what value (if any) that key holds. This is the natural tool for 'has this optional field ever been set' queries -- e.g., WHERE info ? 'discount' finds every product that has a discount field at all, whether its value is 0.10 or 0.99, as opposed to @> which requires matching a specific value.

questions.question: What does `jsonb_to_recordset` allow you to do, and why is it useful for reporting?
options: It converts a relational table into a single JSONB document
It explodes a JSONB array of objects into a relational result set with one row per array element, enabling normal SQL aggregates over previously nested data
It validates a JSONB document against a JSON schema
It deletes all keys from a JSONB document except the ones listed
questions.explanation: Event payloads and API responses often arrive as a JSONB array of objects (e.g., an order's line items). jsonb_to_recordset takes that array and produces one row per object, with columns matching the fields you specify -- letting you run ordinary GROUP BY, SUM, or JOIN operations against data that was previously locked inside a single nested JSONB column, without altering how the data is stored.

questions.question: When is JSONB the appropriate column type, according to the hybrid schema pattern?
options: For every column in every table, to maximize flexibility

For the genuinely variable, read-mostly, schema-evolving portion of a record (preferences, event payloads, config), while frequently-filtered or frequently-updated fields stay as dedicated relational columns
Only for columns smaller than 1 KB
Never -- JSONB should be avoided entirely in production Postgres schemas
questions.explanation: The senior pattern is hybrid: keep fields that are frequently filtered, joined, indexed with B-Tree, or updated often as dedicated typed columns -- they get proper constraints and avoid write amplification. Reserve JSONB for the part of the record that is genuinely variable or evolves faster than a migration process can track, such as user preferences or third-party API payloads whose shape you don't control. Using JSONB for everything forfeits type safety and foreign keys; avoiding it entirely forfeits the flexibility that makes it valuable in the first place.
